title: Reverse-Engineering Model Editing on Language Models
claim: A two-stage procedure first recovers hidden inputs from parameter updates, then their context, while a separate defense blocks this leakage.
layout: 3 regions: attack stage I, stage II, defense; dashed dividers, arrows flow
description: A cream-and-green panel divided by dashed lines into three regions. Top-left (Stage I, subject inference): a prompt template bar is filled with a candidate subject drawn from a cylinder database of coloured cubes, then embedded. The embedding is scored against a subspace plane V, which comes from an SVD of the weight update ΔW (shown as ΔW = UΣVᵀ), computed between blue unedited and orange edited brain icons. This yields a Top-N candidate subjects box. Right (Stage II, prompt recovery): candidate prompt templates, shown as coloured bars, are filled and fed to both brains. An error ratio (E_unedit − E_edit)/E_edit with a funnel 'Select by Ratio' outputs recovered prompts and subjects. Bottom-left (green): the Subspace Camouflage defense merges true and decoy key matrices into an aggregated camouflage key matrix, then edits the LLM. The eye goes first to the brain icons and the colourful bars.
caption: Overview of our proposed two-stage reverse-engineering attack framework KSTER in a white-box setting, along with an associated defense strategy subspace camouflage.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are pretrained on corpora containing trillions of tokens and, therefore, inevitably memorize sensitive information. Locate-then-edit methods, as a mainstream paradigm of model editing, offer a promising solution by modifying model parameters without retraining. However, in this work, we reveal a critical vulnerability of this paradigm: the parameter updates inadvertently serve as a side channel, enabling attackers to recover the edited data. We propose a two-stage reverse-engineering attack named \textit{KSTER} (\textbf{K}ey\textbf{S}paceRecons\textbf{T}ruction-then-\textbf{E}ntropy\textbf{R}eduction) that leverages the low-rank structure of these updates. First, we theoretically show that the row space of the update matrix encodes a ``fingerprint" of the edited subjects, enabling accurate subject recovery via spectral analysis. Second, we introduce an entropy-based prompt recovery attack that reconstructs the semantic context of the edit. Extensive experiments on multiple LLMs demonstrate that our attacks can recover edited data with high success rates. Furthermore, we propose \textit{subspace camouflage}, a defense strategy that obfuscates the update fingerprint with semantic decoys. This approach effectively mitigates reconstruction risks without compromising editing utility. Our code is available at https://github.com/reanatom/EditingAttack.
